title: Classes and Objects (Advanced)
description: Advanced: create your own types with classes, give objects data and actions, and print them nicely.

subLevels.title: Classes and objects
subLevels.summary: Why classes help, and how to make your first one.

blocks.text: So far you have stored data in variables, lists and dictionaries. Data about one thing can end up spread over many variables:

blocks.code:
student1_name = "Asha"
student1_marks = [72, 95]
student2_name = "Ravi"
student2_marks = [64, 81]
print(student1_name, sum(student1_marks))

blocks.text: That works, but it gets messy fast. A class keeps everything about one kind of thing together.

items: A class is a blueprint, like the plan for a house.
An object is one thing built from it, like one house.
One class can make many objects.

blocks.code:
class Dog:
    sound = "Woof"

rex = Dog()
bella = Dog()
rex.name = "Rex"
bella.name = "Bella"
print(rex.name, rex.sound)
print(bella.name, bella.sound)
print(type(rex))
explanation: class Dog: starts the class. Class names use CapitalWords.
Dog() with brackets creates a new object.
A value stored on an object is called an attribute; you read it with a dot.
Each object keeps its own attributes, and __main__ means the class is in your program.

blocks.text: Class = blueprint. Object = one thing made from it, with its own attributes.
Dog() makes a new object. Dog on its own is just the class, the blueprint itself.

blocks.code:
class Dog:
    sound = "Woof"

a = Dog()
b = Dog
print(type(a))
print(type(b))

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Forgetting the brackets: b = Dog stores the class itself, not a new dog. Always write Dog() to create an object.

questions.prompt: Which statement about classes and objects is true?
options: A class and an object are two names for the same thing
A class is a blueprint; an object is one thing made from it
An object is a blueprint; classes are made from it
A class can only ever make one object
questions.explanation: Like a house plan and the houses built from it, one class can make many objects.
questions.hint: Think back to the house plan comparison from the lesson.
optionFeedback: They are different: one is the plan, the other is what's built from it.
Right: blueprint and the thing built from it.
It is the other way round.
One class can make as many objects as you like, like rex and bella.

questions.explanation: tom is a Cat object, so tom.legs reads the legs attribute: 4.
questions.code:
class Cat:
    legs = 4

tom = Cat()
print(tom.legs)
questions.hint: The dot reads a value stored on the object.
optionFeedback: The dot gives the attribute's value, not its name.
Printing an attribute shows its value, not the class name.
tom.legs shows the attribute, not the variable name.
Right: tom.legs is 4.

questions.prompt: This should make a Cat object, but type(pet) shows <class 'type'>. What's wrong?
questions.explanation: Without brackets, pet is the class itself. Cat() creates an object.
questions.code:
class Cat:
    legs = 4

pet = Cat
print(type(pet))
questions.hint: Compare how rex was created in the lesson with how pet is created here.
optionFeedback: Right: brackets create the object.
Class names use CapitalWords, so Cat is right.
4 is a number, so it doesn't need quotes.
type() works on anything; here it shows that pet is a class.

questions.explanation: a has its own colour, red, and every Car has wheels = 4.
questions.code:
class Car:
    wheels = 4

a = Car()
b = Car()
a.colour = "red"
b.colour = "blue"
print(a.colour, b.wheels)
questions.hint: Check which object each attribute is read from.
optionFeedback: a.colour belongs to a, and b's colour doesn't change it.
The second value is b.wheels, not b.colour.
Right: a's colour and b's wheels.
The second value is b.wheels, which is a number.

subLevels.title: __init__ and attributes
subLevels.summary: Set up each object's data when it is created.

blocks.text: Instead of adding attributes one by one, write an __init__ method (two underscores on each side). It runs automatically every time an object is created.

blocks.code:
class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

rex = Dog("Rex", 3)
print(rex.name)
print(rex.age)
explanation: Dog("Rex", 3) creates a Dog and runs __init__.
"Rex" goes to name and 3 goes to age.
self is the new object; self.name = name stores the value on it.

blocks.text: self means "this object". Python fills it in for you: never pass it yourself. Each object gets its own values.

blocks.code:
class Student:
    def __init__(self, name, grade):
        self.name = name
        self.grade = grade

a = Student("Asha", 9)
b = Student("Ravi", 10)
print(a.name, a.grade)
print(b.name, b.grade)

items: Student("Asha", 9): Python makes an empty Student.
It calls __init__ with self = that student, name = "Asha", grade = 9.
self.name = name saves the name on that student.

blocks.code:
class BankAccount:
    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        self.owner = owner
        self.balance = balance

acc = BankAccount("Meera")
print(acc.balance)
acc.balance = 500
print(acc.owner, acc.balance)
explanation: balance=0 is a default value, like in normal functions.
Attributes can be changed later with =.

blocks.text: __init__ gives every new object its starting attributes.
Creating an object must give __init__ every value it asks for, except ones with defaults.

blocks.output: TypeError: Dog.__init__() missing 1 required positional argument: 'age'
explanation: __init__ needs name and age, so creating a Dog needs both values.
blocks.caption: Only the last line of the error is shown.

blocks.text: Inside __init__, the value must be stored on self, or the object never gets it.

blocks.caption: Only the last line of the error is shown.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Forgetting self. in __init__. name = name only changes a local variable, so the object never gets the attribute and reading rex.name gives an AttributeError. Write self.name = name.

blocks.caption: Only the last line of the error is shown.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: __init__ has two underscores before and after. With one, Python doesn't recognise it.

options: Only when you call rex.__init__() yourself
Automatically, every time a new object is created
Once, when the class is written
questions.explanation: Creating an object, like Dog("Rex", 3), runs __init__ for that new object.
questions.hint: Think about what happens straight after you write a class name with brackets.
optionFeedback: Python calls it for you when the object is created.
Right: each new object runs it once.
It runs once per object, not once for the class.
It is about setting up new objects, at the start.

questions.explanation: 700 is passed as pages and stored as self.pages.
questions.hint: Match each value in the brackets to the parameter in the same position.
optionFeedback: Gita is the title; the code prints pages.
Right: b.pages is 700.
The dot gives the value of the attribute, not its name.
b.pages is an attribute value, not the class name.

questions.explanation: self.price = price stores the value on the object being created.
questions.hint: Look at the line just above it, which does the same job for name.
optionFeedback: Item is the class; each object needs its own price.
init is not a name in this code.
Right: self.price stores it on the object.
price = price would only change the local variable.

options: Phone needs brackets in the class line
brand = brand makes a local variable; it should be self.brand = brand
questions.explanation: Without self., the value is never stored on the object, so p.brand gives an AttributeError.
questions.hint: Check whether the value is actually stored on the object inside __init__.
optionFeedback: class Phone: is correct as written.
Attributes can hold any type of value.
print() can show attributes; the attribute just doesn't exist.
Right: self. is missing.

questions.explanation: a uses the default balance 100, b has 50: 100 + 50 = 150.
questions.code:
class Account:
    def __init__(self, owner, balance=100):
        self.owner = owner
        self.balance = balance

a = Account("Asha")
b = Account("Ravi", 50)
print(a.balance + b.balance)
questions.hint: Work out each object's balance separately before adding them.
optionFeedback: That's only a's balance; b's 50 is added too.
b was given 50, so its default of 100 is replaced.
Both balances are numbers, so + adds them.

questions.prompt: Which error does this code cause?
questions.explanation: __init__ needs both name and age, but only one value was given: TypeError (missing argument).
questions.hint: Count the values __init__ needs and compare that with the values given.
optionFeedback: Right: a required argument is missing.
No attribute is read here; the problem is the missing argument.
Dog and rex are both known names.
"Rex" is a fine value; one value is missing.

options: An extra value you must pass, like Dog(self, "Rex")
The new object that is being set up
A variable shared by all objects
questions.explanation: self is the object being created, so self.name belongs to that one object.
questions.hint: Think about where self.name ends up being stored.
optionFeedback: self is one object, not the blueprint.
Python passes self for you; you never write it in the brackets.
Right: self is this object.
Each object has its own self, so values aren't shared.

subLevels.title: Methods
subLevels.summary: Give objects actions with methods that use self.

blocks.text: A method is a function written inside a class. Its first parameter is always self.

explanation: rex.bark() calls the method; Python passes rex in as self.
Inside the method, self.name reads rex's name.
deposit(200) gives amount = 200; self is acc.
Each call adds to the same balance.

items: Methods can take parameters after self.
self.balance += amount changes the object's attribute.

explanation: average() returns a value, like a normal function.
A method can call another method with self.average().

blocks.text: Put the rules inside the method, so every withdrawal is checked the same way.

blocks.output: TypeError: Dog.bark() takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given
blocks.caption: Only the last line of the error is shown.
Only the last line of the error is shown.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Forgetting self. Every method needs self as its first parameter, and inside a method you read attributes with self.name, not name.

questions.explanation: switch() sets self.on to True on lamp.
questions.hint: Follow what each method does to the attribute, in order.
optionFeedback: It started False, but switch() changed it before printing.
lamp.on is an attribute with a value; it was set to a bool.
The code prints the attribute, not the method name.
Right: switch() changed it.

questions.explanation: Both calls add to the same money attribute: 0 + 20 + 30 = 50.
questions.hint: Each call changes the same attribute on the same object.
optionFeedback: Right: 20 + 30.
+= adds to the money, so the first 20 is kept.
The second call adds 30 more.
The method changes self.money, so it doesn't stay 0.

options: bark needs self as its first parameter: def bark(self):
A class needs __init__ before it can have methods
questions.explanation: Python passes rex in as self, but bark() accepts no parameters: TypeError.
questions.hint: Python passes one value to every method call, even with empty brackets.
optionFeedback: Python already passes rex; the method has no parameter to receive it.
Right: add self.
Methods can print like any function.
Methods work without __init__; the missing parameter is the problem.

questions.explanation: Every method's first parameter is self, which gives access to self.width and self.height.
questions.hint: The method body reads attributes through one particular name.
optionFeedback: The values are read from the object, so they aren't parameters.
The class name isn't used as a parameter.
Right: area(self).
Some languages use this, but Python uses a different word.

questions.explanation: area() returns 3 * 4 = 12, and 12 + 1 = 13.
questions.hint: Work out what the method returns, then do the rest of the line.
optionFeedback: Don't forget the + 1 after the method call.
Right: 12 + 1.
area() multiplies, it doesn't add.
area() has a return, so it gives back a number.

questions.explanation: The first take() makes items 0. The second raises ValueError, which is caught, so items stays 0.
questions.hint: Track the value of items after each call, and remember what raise skips.
optionFeedback: Right: the error is printed and items stays 0.
The second take() raises an error, which is caught and printed.
raise stops the method before -= 1 runs.
raise stops the method, and the caught error is printed first.

options: Inside the method it must be self.name, not name
questions.explanation: name only existed inside __init__. Other methods read it from the object as self.name.
questions.hint: Think about where name was stored when the object was set up.
optionFeedback: A method doesn't need return to print.
One parameter is all this Cat needs.
Right: read it from self.
print() can show several values separated by commas.

options: self is a new, empty object each time a method is called
Methods can only read attributes, never change them
When you call rex.bark(), Python passes rex in as self
questions.explanation: The object before the dot becomes self inside the method.
questions.hint: Think about what object is written before the dot in the call.
optionFeedback: Python passes rex automatically, so you never write it.
self is the object the method was called on, with all its attributes.
Methods can change attributes, like deposit() changing balance.
Right: the object before the dot is self.

subLevels.title: Many objects
subLevels.summary: Store objects in lists and work with them together.

blocks.text: Real programs have many objects: a class of students, a cart of items. Keep them in a list.

blocks.code:
class Student:
    def __init__(self, name, mark):
        self.name = name
        self.mark = mark

students = [Student("Asha", 82), Student("Ravi", 67), Student("Meera", 91)]
total = 0
best = students[0]
for s in students:
    print(s.name, s.mark)
    total += s.mark
    if s.mark > best.mark:
        best = s
print("Average:", total / len(students))
print("Top:", best.name)
print([s.name for s in students if s.mark >= 70])
blocks.output:
Asha 82
Ravi 67
Meera 91
Average: 80.0
Top: Meera
['Asha', 'Meera']
explanation: A list can hold objects like any other value.
The loop variable s is one Student at a time.
best remembers the student with the highest mark so far.

items: Make many objects by calling the class many times.
Keep them in a list and loop over it.
Use the dot on the loop variable: s.name.

pages.title: Same object or a new one?

blocks.code:
class Counter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.count = 0

a = Counter()
b = a
c = Counter()
b.count = 5
print(a.count, b.count, c.count)
explanation: b = a doesn't copy: a and b are two names for the same object.
c = Counter() is a separate object, so it still has 0.

blocks.text: Calling the class makes a new object; = only gives an existing object another name.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Thinking b = a makes a copy. Changing b.count also changes a.count, because they are the same object. Call the class again to get a separate object.

questions.explanation: The loop adds each item's price: 10 + 40 = 50.
questions.hint: Each round of the loop adds one object's price to total.
optionFeedback: Right: 10 + 40.
The loop adds prices, not a count of items.
The prices are numbers, so they are added.
Only total is printed, and it holds prices.

questions.explanation: y = x makes y another name for the same Box, so changing y.size changes x.size.
questions.code:
class Box:
    def __init__(self):
        self.size = 1

x = Box()
y = x
y.size = 9
print(x.size)
questions.hint: Ask whether y = x creates a second object or not.
optionFeedback: Right: x and y are the same object.
y = x didn't make a copy, so x changed too.
size was replaced with 9, not increased.
x has a size attribute, set in __init__.

questions.explanation: Only pets older than 2 are kept, and their names are collected.
questions.hint: Check each pet's age against the condition, then look at what is collected.
optionFeedback: Tom is 1, so he fails the condition.
Right: Rex and Bo are older than 2.
The if keeps only some pets.
The list collects p.name, not p.age.

questions.explanation: a and b are separate objects: a ticked twice and b once.
questions.code:
class Counter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.n = 0

    def tick(self):
        self.n += 1

a = Counter()
b = Counter()
a.tick()
a.tick()
b.tick()
print(a.n, b.n)
questions.hint: Each object made by calling the class keeps its own count.
optionFeedback: Each object has its own n; they don't share it.
a.tick() was called twice.
b.tick() was called only once.
Right: they count separately.

options: b = a makes a copy of the object a
All objects of a class share their attributes set in __init__
Calling the class again, like Dog("Bella"), always makes a new, separate object
A list can only hold one object of each class
questions.explanation: Each call to the class makes a new object. = only adds another name.
questions.hint: Think about the difference between c and b in the Counter example.
optionFeedback: b = a gives the same object a second name.
Attributes set with self belong to each object.
Right: a new call, a new object.
A list can hold as many objects as you like.

subLevels.title: Printing objects and why classes
subLevels.summary: Use __str__ to print objects nicely, and see why classes help.

blocks.text: Printing an object you made shows something like <__main__.Dog object at 0x7f...>. The number is a memory address, so it changes from run to run.

blocks.caption: Prints something like <__main__.Dog object at 0x7f3a2c1d5e90>.

blocks.text: Add a __str__ method to choose the text yourself. It must return a string.

blocks.output:
Rex (3 years)
My dog: Rex (3 years)
Hello Rex (3 years)
explanation: print(), str() and f-strings all use __str__ to turn the object into text.

blocks.caption: Only the last line of the error is shown.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Printing inside __str__ instead of returning the text. __str__ must return a string; if it returns nothing, you get a TypeError.

items: Data and actions stay together: the balance lives with deposit().
Rules live in one place: every deposit is checked.

blocks.text: Use a class when you have several things of the same kind, each with its own data and actions.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Classes can do much more, but you now know enough to organise real programs with them.

questions.explanation: print(f) uses __str__, which returns "Fruit: " + self.name.
questions.hint: Printing an object uses the text that one special method returns.
optionFeedback: __str__ adds Fruit: in front of the name.
__str__ includes the name as well.
Right: __str__ chooses the text.
Because there is a __str__, Python uses it instead of the default text.

options: When the object is printed or turned into text with str()
Only when you write obj.__str__() yourself
questions.explanation: print(), str() and f-strings call __str__ to get the object's text.
questions.hint: Think about the three lines in the lesson that all showed the same text.
optionFeedback: Right: whenever text is needed.
Creating an object runs __init__, not __str__.
Changing attributes doesn't print anything.
Python calls it for you, for example inside print().

options: __str__ must return the text instead of printing it
questions.explanation: This __str__ prints and returns nothing (None), so Python raises a TypeError.
questions.hint: Look at what the special method gives back to Python.
optionFeedback: __str__ only needs self.
Objects can be printed, especially with a working __str__.
Printing the class wouldn't print the dog.
Right: replace print with return.

questions.explanation: __str__ must give back a string with return.
questions.hint: The special method has to hand a string back to Python.
optionFeedback: Right: return the text.
print shows text but gives back None, which causes a TypeError.
Storing it in an attribute doesn't give it back.
str on its own does nothing with the text.

questions.explanation: The f-string puts p in the text using its __str__, which returns Asha=7.
questions.hint: An f-string turns the object into text the same way print() does.
optionFeedback: The f in front fills in {p}.
Right: the f-string uses __str__.
{p} is replaced with the object's text, not its name.
__str__ includes the score too.

options: It makes programs run without any errors
It keeps related data and the actions that use it together
Every Python program must use a class
Classes are needed to use lists and dictionaries
questions.explanation: A class bundles data (attributes) and actions (methods), like balance and deposit().
questions.hint: Think about what the BankAccount class kept in one place.
optionFeedback: Classes can still have errors, like a missing self.
Right: data and actions together.
Most of this course worked without classes.
